specPoints.text: know that light waves are transverse waves and that they can be reflected and refracted
know that sound waves are longitudinal waves which can be reflected and refracted

primer.text: The wave families from earlier now earn their places in optics: light is the transverse wave you see by, sound the longitudinal wave you hear by. Both can bounce off surfaces and bend between media, and each is drawn with its own diagram style. This lesson pairs the two and shows how each is represented.

lessons.title: Light waves
lessons.opening: Light belongs to the electromagnetic spectrum, so it is a transverse wave: its fields vibrate across the direction of travel, the way a drawn wave on a rope does. Two things light famously does at surfaces and boundaries are reflection and refraction, both of which get their own diagrams later in this topic.
keyPoints: A transverse wave is drawn as a wavy line with peaks and troughs.

low.restatement: Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave, which is why it is drawn with the peak-and-trough style and why it bounces and bends at boundaries.
low.analogy: Light behaves like the rope wave: shake across the path, travel along it.
low.examPointer: When asked for the wave type of light, answer transverse and be ready to add electromagnetic for the second mark.

medium.restatement: Being transverse and electromagnetic lets light cross vacuum and still reflect and refract at boundaries, since those behaviours depend on wavefronts meeting media changes rather than on the medium carrying the wave.
medium.analogy: A courier who needs no road (vacuum) but still turns at every junction (boundary).
medium.examPointer: Link questions: light is transverse because it is EM; it crosses vacuum for the same reason.

options.explanation: That is the sound family.
Light is part of the electromagnetic spectrum, which is transverse.
Light needs no material medium.
Pressure waves are longitudinal.

check.stem: Which two behaviours can light undergo at boundaries?

options.explanation: Those are longitudinal-wave regions, not behaviours.
Those are interaction effects, not the listed boundary behaviours.
The note lists exactly these two for light.
Absorption is not the pair the spec names here.

check.stem: A transverse wave is represented in a diagram as:

options.text: lines of varying spacing along the travel direction
options.explanation: That is the longitudinal representation.
A ray arrow shows direction, not the wave shape.
No spiral representation is used here.

options.text: a wavy line with peaks and troughs
options.explanation: The peak-and-trough profile is the transverse picture.

check.stem: Light can travel from the Sun to the Earth through space. This is possible because light:

options.text: is electromagnetic and needs no medium
options.explanation: EM waves cross vacuum without particles.

options.text: borrows air particles along the way
options.explanation: Space has no particles to borrow.

options.text: slows to a stop without a medium
options.explanation: Light crosses vacuum at its full free-space speed.
Light is transverse and space is not squeezed.

check.stem: A light ray hits a glass surface partly bouncing back and partly passing in bent. The two behaviours are called:

options.explanation: Those are different wave behaviours outside this pairing.
Those are sound terms.
Bouncing back is reflection; bending on entry is refraction.
Dispersion is colour splitting, not this pair.

check.stem: State the wave family of light and the drawing style used for it.
check.modelAnswer: Light is a transverse (electromagnetic) wave, drawn as a wavy line with peaks and troughs.

check.stem: State the two boundary behaviours of light named in the note.
Explain why light is drawn as a transverse wave rather than with compression lines.
check.modelAnswer: Light belongs to the electromagnetic spectrum, and all EM waves are transverse, so the peak-and-trough drawing shows its crosswise vibration while compression lines would falsely suggest a longitudinal push-pull wave.

check.stem: A camera flash reflects off a window into a driver’s eyes, and the same beam bends as it passes into the glass. Identify each behaviour and the wave family involved.
check.modelAnswer: The bounce at the window is reflection and the bend on entering the glass is refraction; both happen to light, a transverse electromagnetic wave.

lessons.title: Sound waves
lessons.opening: Sound is the longitudinal partner: air particles shuffle along the travel direction, forming compressions and rarefactions that are drawn as lines packed close together and spread apart. Like light, sound can reflect, heard as an echo, and refract between media, though it always needs a material to travel in.
keyPoints: Sound can be reflected; the reflection of a sound wave is called an echo.
Longitudinal waves are drawn as lines along the travel direction, with close lines showing compressions and spread lines showing rarefactions.

low.restatement: Sound is a longitudinal wave, drawn as lines that bunch and spread along the direction of travel, and its reflection arrives at your ears as an echo.
low.analogy: A slinky pushed lengthways: squeezed zones and stretched zones chasing each other down the coils.
low.examPointer: Name the echo explicitly when a question mentions reflected sound; the vocabulary is the mark.

medium.restatement: Because sound is mechanical and longitudinal, it shares reflection and refraction with light yet differs in needing particles, so the same boundary diagrams apply with the medium, not vacuum, doing the carrying.
medium.analogy: Light and sound are two couriers through a building: same turns taken, but one needs corridors with air and one does not.
medium.examPointer: Contrast questions love the vacuum difference: sound dies in space, light does not; quote the particle requirement.

options.explanation: That is the light family.
Sound particles vibrate along the travel direction.
Sound is mechanical, not electromagnetic.
Sound cannot travel in vacuum at all.

check.stem: A sound wave that bounces back from a surface is called:

options.explanation: That is a wave region, not a reflection.
That is a drawing line, not a reflection.
That belongs to light.
Echo is the standard name for reflected sound.

check.stem: On a longitudinal wave diagram, compressions are shown by:

options.explanation: Bunched lines represent the crowded compression regions.
Wide spacing shows rarefactions.
Peaks belong to transverse drawings.
No dotted convention is used here.

check.stem: Sound can undergo which boundary behaviours?

options.explanation: Refraction of sound is also listed.
That is an EM interaction, not a sound behaviour.
The note lists both for sound, as for light.
That is an ultraviolet effect.

check.stem: Sound cannot reach us from space because:

options.text: sound is too fast for space
options.explanation: Speed is irrelevant; the medium is the problem.
Light crosses space perfectly well.
Refraction needs a boundary between media; there is nothing to refract in.

options.text: sound needs particles and space has almost none
options.explanation: Longitudinal mechanical waves require a material medium.

check.stem: State the wave family of sound and its everyday reflected form.
check.modelAnswer: Sound is a longitudinal wave; its reflection is heard as an echo.

check.stem: State how rarefactions appear on a longitudinal wave diagram.
check.modelAnswer: Rarefactions appear as lines drawn further apart, showing the spread-out regions.

check.stem: Explain why the drawing styles for light and sound differ.
check.modelAnswer: Light is transverse so its crosswise vibration is drawn as a peak-and-trough line, while sound is longitudinal so its along-the-line push-pull is drawn as bunched and spaced lines; each style encodes the true vibration direction of its family.

check.stem: A swimmer clicks two stones together underwater and hears the click reflected from the pool wall. Identify the wave family, the reflected sound and one behaviour the click shares with light at the water surface.
check.modelAnswer: The click is a longitudinal sound wave; its wall reflection is an echo; at the water surface the click also refracts, bending between media just as light does.

glossary.definition: The reflection of a sound wave heard after the original sound.
The closely spaced lines drawn to represent compressed regions of a longitudinal wave.
The spread-out region of a longitudinal wave between two compressions.
